heuristics.rule: California 6-month state residency requirement for divorce filing
heuristics.condition: When a spouse wishes to file for divorce in California...
heuristics.action: At least one spouse must have lived in California for the last 6 months before filing
heuristics.because: California courts require established residency to assert jurisdiction over a dissolution of marriage proceeding
heuristics.regulatory_basis: California Courts Self-Help Center (Judicial Branch of California), selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california

heuristics.rule: California 3-month county residency requirement for divorce filing
heuristics.condition: When a spouse wishes to file for divorce in a specific California county...
heuristics.action: At least one spouse must have resided in that specific California county for the last 3 months before filing
heuristics.because: California courts require county-level residency to determine the proper local court venue for filing
heuristics.regulatory_basis: California Courts Self-Help Center (Judicial Branch of California), selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california

heuristics.rule: Mandatory wait when neither spouse meets California residency requirement
heuristics.condition: When neither spouse has met the 6-month state and 3-month county residency requirements...
heuristics.action: Both spouses must generally wait until the residency requirement is met before filing in California
heuristics.because: Filing eligibility is contingent on satisfying both residency thresholds; no exception or waiver is stated in the official guidance
heuristics.regulatory_basis: California Courts Self-Help Center (Judicial Branch of California), selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california

heuristics.rule: No-fault filing: spousal agreement not required
heuristics.condition: When a spouse wants to file for divorce in California...
heuristics.action: The filing spouse does not need the other spouse's agreement and does not need to prove wrongdoing; divorce may be filed for any reason
heuristics.because: California operates under a no-fault model: 'You don't need your spouse's agreement to get a divorce. You can get divorced for any reason.'
heuristics.regulatory_basis: California Courts Self-Help Center (Judicial Branch of California), selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california

heuristics.rule: Separate treatment of 'whether to leave' vs. 'how to legally leave'
heuristics.condition: When advising someone on ending a relationship who has recently relocated to a new state...
heuristics.action: Surface the residency window requirement as a concrete, checkable fact before discussing filing mechanics — do not conflate emotional/repairability diagnosis with legal eligibility
heuristics.because: Residency requirements create a real eligibility gate that affects when and where a person can file; the two questions require different information
heuristics.regulatory_basis: California Courts Self-Help Center (Judicial Branch of California), selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether California has jurisdiction to hear the divorce filing; filing before meeting this threshold is not permitted
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Verify that at least one spouse has lived continuously in California for the last 6 months prior to intended filing date

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines the proper venue (specific court) within California; a separate 3-month requirement from the state-level requirement
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Verify that at least one spouse has resided in the specific California county for the last 3 months prior to intended filing date

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Only one spouse needs to meet the requirements, not both; this affects who initiates the filing and in which county
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess each spouse's individual residency history independently — either spouse's qualifying residency is sufficient

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Under California's no-fault model, the reason for filing is legally irrelevant to eligibility; no proof of wrongdoing is required
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Not a determining factor in California; any reason suffices and no fault needs to be established

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A spouse who recently moved to California or to a new county within California may not yet satisfy the 6-month or 3-month residency windows, creating a filing delay
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate the date the spouse established California and county residency and determine whether the required intervals have elapsed

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Filing for divorce immediately after relocating to California
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Filing is not permitted until both the 6-month state and 3-month county residency requirements are independently satisfied; early relocation does not accelerate eligibility
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who have recently moved to California (e.g., for employment, family, or immigration-related reasons) and wish to file without delay

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming no-fault means no procedural requirements
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: No-fault eliminates the need to prove wrongdoing but does not eliminate residency thresholds; procedural eligibility gates (6 months state, 3 months county) remain fully in force
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Any spouse who conflates the ease of the no-fault substantive standard with the procedural residency requirements

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on California's residency rules as universally representative
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Residency windows vary by state (commonly 3–12 months depending on state) and terminology differs ('dissolution of marriage' vs. 'divorce'); California's specific thresholds do not apply in other states
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Spouses who have recently moved from California to another state, or who assume California rules apply nationally

failure_patterns.pattern: Filing for divorce in California before satisfying the 6-month state residency requirement
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Filer or both spouses have not yet lived in California for the required 6-month period prior to filing
failure_patterns.consequence: Filing is not permitted; spouses must wait until the residency requirement is met
warning_signs: Spouse recently relocated to California (less than 6 months ago)
Neither spouse has a continuous 6-month California residency history prior to the intended filing date

failure_patterns.pattern: Filing for divorce in a California county before satisfying the 3-month county residency requirement
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Filer has met the 6-month state requirement but has not yet lived in the specific county for 3 months
failure_patterns.consequence: Filing in that county is not permitted; filer must wait until the 3-month county threshold is met
warning_signs: Spouse recently moved to a new county within California (less than 3 months ago)
State residency is established but county residency is not yet 3 months

failure_patterns.pattern: Conflating emotional readiness to leave with legal eligibility to file
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Decision to leave and legal mechanics of filing are treated as a single question rather than two separate axes
failure_patterns.consequence: Person is unprepared for the residency waiting period and cannot file when expected, delaying legal proceedings
warning_signs: Person asks 'how do I leave' immediately after a recent interstate or international move without first checking residency eligibility
Person assumes decision to divorce is sufficient to initiate filing without verifying residency thresholds

diagnostic_questions.question: Has at least one spouse lived in California continuously for the last 6 months?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the state-level residency requirement for California divorce filing is satisfied
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Proceed to assess the 3-month county residency requirement
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Filing in California is not currently permitted; calculate when the 6-month threshold will be reached

diagnostic_questions.question: Has at least one spouse resided in their current California county for the last 3 months?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the county-level venue requirement for California divorce filing is satisfied
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Both residency requirements are met; the spouse may file in that county
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Filing in that specific county is not yet permitted; calculate when the 3-month county threshold will be reached

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the person recently relocated to a new state or a new county within California?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a residency waiting period is an active constraint on filing timeline
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Surface the residency window requirements as a concrete eligibility gate before discussing filing mechanics
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Residency is likely established; verify exact move-in dates to confirm both thresholds are met

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the person asking whether to leave the relationship, or how to file for divorce given their current location?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the relevant information needed is emotional/repairability diagnosis or legal/procedural filing mechanics — these are distinct questions requiring different information
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If asking 'how to file': assess residency eligibility first before discussing process
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If asking 'whether to leave': address repairability diagnosis without conflating legal filing mechanics

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the filing spouse believe they need the other spouse's consent or must prove fault to obtain a divorce in California?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person understands California's no-fault model, which requires neither spousal agreement nor proof of wrongdoing
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Clarify that California's no-fault model explicitly states: 'You don't need your spouse's agreement to get a divorce. You can get divorced for any reason.'
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Person already understands no-fault basis; focus on procedural residency requirements

industry_realities.common_belief: You can file for divorce in California at any time once you decide to end the marriage
industry_realities.actual_reality: Filing requires one spouse to have lived in California for at least 6 months AND in the specific county for at least 3 months; neither condition can be waived by mutual agreement or immediate intent to file
industry_realities.implication: Anyone who has recently moved to California or to a new county must calculate the earliest eligible filing date before initiating divorce proceedings

industry_realities.common_belief: No-fault divorce means there are no procedural requirements or waiting periods
industry_realities.actual_reality: No-fault eliminates the requirement to prove wrongdoing and removes the need for spousal consent, but residency requirements (6 months state, 3 months county) are separate procedural thresholds that remain fully in effect
industry_realities.implication: Spouses must satisfy both residency thresholds regardless of how clear-cut or uncontested the no-fault grounds are

industry_realities.common_belief: California's divorce residency rules represent the national standard
industry_realities.actual_reality: The official source explicitly states that residency windows vary by state, commonly ranging from 3 to 12 months depending on the state, and that terminology also varies ('dissolution of marriage' vs. 'divorce')
industry_realities.implication: Spouses who have moved from California to another state must research that specific state's residency requirement rather than assuming California's 6-month/3-month thresholds apply

industry_realities.common_belief: The decision to leave a relationship and the ability to file for divorce are the same question
industry_realities.actual_reality: The official source explicitly identifies these as two separate axes: 'A user asking should I leave and a user asking how do I actually leave, given I just moved states are asking different questions that require different information'
industry_realities.implication: Advisors and individuals must address emotional/repairability diagnosis and legal/procedural eligibility as distinct inquiries, not a single combined question

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of when divorce filing can begin
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes filing can start immediately once both parties (or one party) decides the marriage is over, without checking residency history
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Immediately checks whether the 6-month state and 3-month county residency thresholds are satisfied before discussing any filing timeline or process
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Filing before meeting residency requirements is not permitted; failure to check creates false expectations about when proceedings can begin

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats no-fault as meaning there are no barriers or requirements to filing — just a simple decision to proceed
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Understands that no-fault eliminates the fault-proving requirement and spousal consent requirement but does not eliminate the independent residency eligibility thresholds
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Conflating no-fault ease with absence of procedural requirements leads to premature or improperly filed petitions

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Proceeds directly to explaining divorce process mechanics without surfacing the residency window as a threshold eligibility issue
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats residency eligibility as a concrete, checkable fact to be surfaced first — before any discussion of 'how' to file — especially for someone who has recently moved states or counties
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A recently relocated person may face a mandatory waiting period before they can file; not surfacing this creates a gap between advice given and what the person can actually do

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Distinguishing 'whether to leave' from 'how to leave legally'
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats both questions as part of the same conversation and provides a single combined answer covering emotional readiness and legal process simultaneously
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Recognizes these as two separate axes requiring different information — emotional/repairability diagnosis is distinct from legal filing eligibility — and addresses each independently
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Conflating the two questions can result in providing legally irrelevant information to someone with an emotional decision question, or emotionally focused advice to someone with a concrete legal eligibility problem

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Generalizing California rules to other states
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Applies California's 6-month/3-month residency rule as if it were a national standard applicable in all US states
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows that residency windows vary by state (commonly 3–12 months) and that even terminology differs by state; treats California's thresholds as California-specific, not universally representative
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Applying the wrong state's residency threshold to a filing in a different state produces incorrect eligibility assessments and filing timelines
